428.title: The sky is the platter
428.hook: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: creation performs the aarti (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
428.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly within Kirtan Sohila, and gurdwaras also sing it on its own in the evening as the Aarti, usually without lamps, while a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of hymn three, and your line: gagan mai thaal. Did you look up for one breath last night? Today, what the platter is for. Day four hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `GAGAN MAI THAAL — THE SKY, A PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Evening at a Hindu temple. The bells start. A priest lifts a brass tray with small flames burning on it and moves it in slow circles before the image of the deity. Incense curls up. Someone waves a fan of white hair. Flowers lie heaped at the front. People sing, clap, reach toward the flames and draw the warmth back over their eyes. That's an aarti. Sohila's third hymn takes the items on that tray and finds each one, much larger, somewhere in the world.
screen: `A BRASS TRAY OF FLAMES.` → `INCENSE, A FAN, FLOWERS.` → `EVERY ITEM, FOUND IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Aarti is the waving of lamps, a way of honoring what is dear by circling light before it. Now walk through the hymn with the tray in mind. The platter: the sky. The lamps: the sun and the moon. Then: taarika mandal janak moti, the circles of stars are like pearls scattered across it. More items follow, the incense, the fan, the flowers, and we'll take those tomorrow. Then the refrain. In paraphrase: what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear; this is Your aarti. And the unstruck sound, the music no hand plays, sounds like the temple drums. So who is performing the aarti? Not a priest. Creation itself. In the hymn, the whole universe, every evening, is lifting its lamps toward the One. In Sikh practice the hymn itself is sung as the aarti, with no tray and no flames: the sound is the offering. A few historic gurdwaras also keep an evening ceremony with lamps alongside the singing, and Sikhs differ on that practice. Both share the line's big picture: the offering is already happening, all around, all the time. You don't light it. You notice it.
screen: `AARTI: CIRCLING LIGHT IN HONOR.` · `SKY, SUN AND MOON, STARS AS PEARLS.` · `WHAT A WONDERFUL AARTI THIS IS.` · `CREATION ITSELF IS OFFERING.` · then, large: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky. If it's dark where you are, go to a window or step outside. Find the moon if it's up, or one star, or even the orange glow of a city sky. Let your eyes rest there. Picture that sky as a tray held up in honor, and you standing underneath it as one of the people at the edge of the crowd. If it's daytime, look at the sky as it is and remember it'll be lit differently tonight. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Aarti. The offering of circling lamps; in Sohila's third hymn, the aarti the whole creation performs, with the sky as its platter.
Your line: the sky is the platter. Today, catch one ordinary thing, a streetlight, a sunset on a window, a flower by a curb, and see it as an item on the tray. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: The wind as incense
429.hook: tradition sets this hymn at Puri, where Nanak saw a temple aarti and pointed to the one the universe performs
429.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly in Kirtan Sohila and sing it in gurdwaras as the Aarti; the story of Guru Nanak at Puri is often told alongside it, especially at gurdwara evening programs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarti, and your line: the sky is the platter. Did you catch one ordinary thing and see it on the tray? Today, the story Sikhs tell about where this hymn was first sung. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

The east coast of India, the Bay of Bengal. A town called Puri, home to the great temple of Jagannath, Lord of the World. Pilgrims still walk there. The janamsakhis, the old collections of stories about Guru Nanak's life, say he came here on his long journeys, with his companion Mardana, the musician who played the rabab. Evening came, and the temple's aarti began: lamps on golden trays, incense, bells, crowds. And the stories say that Guru Nanak stood quietly and didn't join in.
screen: `PURI, ON THE BAY OF BENGAL.` → `NANAK AND MARDANA ARRIVE.` → `THE EVENING AARTI BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In one telling, someone notices the visitor standing apart and asks why he isn't taking part in the aarti. In reply, Guru Nanak asks Mardana to play, and he sings: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The fragrant breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, the forests are the flowers. What a wonderful aarti this is. The aarti, he says, has been going on the whole time. It's just bigger than the temple. Hold this story as tradition. The hymn itself doesn't name Puri, and the janamsakhis were written down after Guru Nanak's lifetime and don't always agree in detail. What the hymn does say is in its later verses, and they turn the picture inside out. In paraphrase: You have thousands of eyes, and yet no eye. Thousands of forms, and yet not one form. Thousands of feet, yet no foot; thousands of noses, yet no nose. And then: within everything is a light, and that light is You. By that light, all are lit. So the wind isn't only incense. The wind, the stars, the forests, the people at the temple, the people standing apart: all of them are lit by the same light. The story, as Sikhs tell it, isn't about scorning anybody's lamps. It shows Guru Nanak widening the circle until the whole world is inside the offering, the priests, the pilgrims and the two travelers too.
screen: `WHY AREN'T YOU JOINING IN?` · `THE AARTI HAS BEEN GOING ON ALL ALONG.` · `THOUSANDS OF EYES, YET NO EYE.` · `ONE LIGHT, AND ALL ARE LIT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smell the evening air. Open a window, or step outside, or simply breathe in slowly where you are. What's in it? Cut grass, rain, exhaust, someone's cooking, the dryness of an air conditioner. Whatever it is, let it be the incense in the hymn, carried to you on the wind. Breathe it in, and breathe out slowly. Then once more, a little slower. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
The wind as incense. In Sohila's third hymn, the breeze carries the fragrance and the wind waves the fan: the whole world performing the aarti.
Your line: the whole world offering. Today, when you feel a breeze or catch a smell on the air, let it remind you that the aarti, in the hymn's picture, never stops. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

430.title: Hymn 4, sound: kaam karodh
430.hook: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)
430.howItsDone: This is the fourth of the five hymns Sikhs recite every night in Kirtan Sohila; it is Guru Ram Das's, and it follows the three hymns of Guru Nanak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story of Puri, and your line: the whole world offering. Did a breeze remind you of the aarti that never stops? Today the mood changes. Hymn four. Day four hundred thirty.

A new voice enters Sohila tonight. The first three hymns were Guru Nanak's. The fourth is by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, whom Sikhs remember as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. Someone who founds a town learns how one fills up, street by street. So it fits that his hymn is about a town, and a crowded one. Only this town isn't on any map. It's a body at the end of a long day, with whatever it's still carrying. And his first line sounds like a warning.
screen: `A NEW VOICE: GURU RAM DAS.` → `A TOWN, AND A CROWDED ONE.` → `THE FIRST LINE IS A WARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Word by word. Kaam: desire that has run out of control, lust, craving. Karodh: anger. Nagar: a town, a city. Bahu: very much, greatly. Bhariaa: filled. So: the city is crammed with desire and anger. The city is the body, and the mind that lives in it. That's the picture: a crowded town, its streets full of two restless characters who never seem to sleep. Then the line finishes, and the warning becomes a hope. In paraphrase: meeting the holy, they are broken to pieces. The holy here is saadhoo, the person who has truly given themselves to God, and some readers hear in it the sangat, the company of people who sing God's praise together. So the hymn doesn't pretend the city is quiet. It names the crowd, and it names what breaks it up. The hymn is in Raag Gauri Purbi and sits on Ang 13, right after Guru Nanak's three. Here's something to notice about its sound. Kaam and karodh both open on a hard k. The line begins with a jolt, like a door banged at night. It's hard to sleep through. Tomorrow we'll walk through the whole city and meet the rest of its residents. Today, just let the first line land: two loud names, a crowded town, and the promise that the crowd can be broken.
screen: `KAAM: CRAVING. KARODH: ANGER.` · `NAGAR: THE CITY OF THE BODY.` · `MEETING THE HOLY, THEY BREAK.` · `A LINE THAT OPENS WITH A JOLT.` · then, large: `KAAM KARODH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Say it once, clearly, and feel the two hard k sounds at the start. Then say it again, more softly. Now sit for a moment and notice, without judging, whether either of those two is in your city right now. A little irritation from the day? A craving for something? Just notice it, the way you'd notice a car passing outside. Then breathe slowly and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Hymn 4. Sohila's fourth hymn, by Guru Ram Das: the city of the body is crammed with desire and anger, and meeting the holy, they are broken.
Your line: kaam karodh. Desire and anger. Today, if one of them shows up loud, name it quietly in your head, just the word, and see what naming it does. Day four hundred thirty.

431.title: A city full of thieves
431.hook: the body is a city crowded with lust and anger; meeting the holy, they are broken (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)
431.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn every night in Kirtan Sohila, and the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, hankaar) are a staple of Sikh teaching, answered by Naam, seva and the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first line of hymn four, and your line: kaam karodh, desire and anger. Did naming one of them change anything? Today, the whole city. Day four hundred thirty-one.

Lights off. Phone face down. The body exhausted, the mind wide awake. It replays an argument from lunch. It scrolls through something it wants and can't have. It drafts the perfect reply that will never be sent. The room is quiet, but the city inside is not. There's a crowd in there, and none of them got the memo that it's bedtime. Sohila's fourth hymn is recited at exactly that hour, and it names two of the loudest in the crowd.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `THE CITY INSIDE IS NOT.` → `TWO OF THEM HAVE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Another hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib names the whole crowd plainly: in this body live five thieves, chor. Kaam, desire out of control. Krodh, anger. Lobh, greed. Moh, clinging attachment. And hankaar, ego, pride. That hymn says they plunder the nectar inside. In plain terms, they steal attention, peace, the hours meant for something better. This hymn names the first two, crowding the city. Then it shows the deeper problem. In paraphrase: the faithless one never tastes the sweetness of God; inside them is the thorn of ego, and the more they walk, the more it pricks. That's a picture anyone with a splinter in their foot understands. You can keep walking, but every step hurts, and the cause is inside. So how is the city cleared? Not by force. The hymn's answer is humility and company. In paraphrase: greet the holy with joined palms, a great merit; bow before them, a great merit. Meeting the holy, desire and anger break apart. And God's humble servants merge in the Name, and the pain of birth and death is broken. For Sikhs, the holy company is sangat, people gathered to sing God's praise. Notice the hymn doesn't picture anyone fighting the thieves alone in the dark. It pictures joined palms, a bowed head, and good company. The city clears because better company moves in.
screen: `FIVE THIEVES THAT STEAL YOUR PEACE.` · `THE THORN OF EGO PRICKS EACH STEP.` · `JOINED PALMS, A BOWED HEAD.` · `BETTER COMPANY MOVES IN.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thief to evict. Sit comfortably. Go through the five slowly: desire, anger, greed, clinging, pride. Which one has been loudest in your city this week? Don't argue with it. Just name it, quietly. Now picture opening the city gate and letting it walk out, the way you'd show a guest who stayed too long to the door. Breathe out as it goes. Then sit in the quieter street it leaves behind. If you pray, you can join your palms for a moment. The bell holds the time.
A city full of thieves. Sohila's fourth hymn: the body crowded with desire and anger, the thorn of ego inside, and the holy company that clears the streets.
screen: `A CITY FULL OF THIEVES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: clear the city. Today, spend ten minutes with someone who makes you calmer, in person or on the phone, and notice which thief goes quiet. Day four hundred thirty-one.

432.title: Hymn 5, sound: karau benantee
432.hook: karau benantee sunahu mere meetaa (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)
432.howItsDone: This is the fifth and final hymn of Kirtan Sohila, which Sikhs recite each night before sleep; in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is then laid to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city full of thieves, and your line: clear the city. Did ten minutes in good company quiet one of them? Today, Sohila's last hymn. Day four hundred thirty-two.

There's a particular tone people use when something really matters. Not a speech. Not a lecture. A friend leaning across the table, lowering their voice: listen, can I ask you something? It's the tone that gets a phone put down. The last hymn of Sohila opens in that voice. After the crowded city of the fourth hymn, the fifth doesn't raise its voice at all. It turns to the listener, calls them friend, and asks for their attention. And it's a third Guru's voice: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru.
screen: `LISTEN, CAN I ASK YOU SOMETHING?` → `THE LAST HYMN LOWERS ITS VOICE.` → `A THIRD GURU: GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Word by word. Karau: I make, I offer. Benantee: a humble request, a plea. You may know the everyday Punjabi word benti, the same thing: a heartfelt request. Sunahu: listen. Mere: my. Meetaa: friends. So: I make a request; listen, my friends. Notice who's speaking to whom. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, the scripture Sikhs now honor as the Guru Granth Sahib. He could have opened with authority. Instead he opens like someone asking a favor, and he calls the listeners friends, not followers. Then the line goes on, and the request turns out to be urgent. In paraphrase: this is the time to serve the holy. We'll open that tomorrow. For now, notice the shape Sohila has built. Five hymns, three Gurus. Guru Nanak wrote the first three: the house of praise, the six schools and one sun, the sky's aarti. Guru Ram Das wrote the fourth, the city full of thieves. Guru Arjan wrote the fifth, this one. The first is in a form of Raag Gauri, the second in Asa, the third in Dhanasri, and the last two share Gauri Purbi. It's a little anthology in one night prayer, and it ends not with a doctrine but with a friend saying: please, listen.
screen: `KARAU BENANTEE: I MAKE A REQUEST.` · `SUNAHU MERE MEETAA: LISTEN, FRIENDS.` · `FRIENDS, NOT FOLLOWERS.` · `FIVE HYMNS, THREE GURUS.` · then, large: `KARAU BENANTEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the first line aloud. Karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Say it once in an ordinary voice. Then say it again in the voice you'd use with a close friend you were worried about: lower, slower, closer. Notice how different it sounds. Then sit quietly and imagine the line being said to you, by someone who wants good for you. Just listen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Hymn 5. Sohila's last hymn, by Guru Arjan in Raag Gauri Purbi, which opens with a plea: I make a request; listen, my friends.
Your line: karau benantee. I make a request. Today, when you need to ask someone for something important, try asking the way the hymn does: as a friend, not a boss. Day four hundred thirty-two.

433.title: Now is the time
433.hook: listen, friends: now is the time to serve the holy and earn the Name (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)
433.tomorrow: A wedding song at a funeral
433.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn as the last of Kirtan Sohila every night, so its call that now is the time to serve and remember is often the final teaching heard before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first line of hymn five, and your line: karau benantee, I make a request. Did you ask for something as a friend would? Today, what the request actually is. Day four hundred thirty-three.

A caravan halts at a market town. For a few days there's buying and selling, haggling and loading, and then the caravan moves on. Everyone knows the rule: what you earn here is what you carry home. Spend the market days sleeping, or gambling, or arguing, and you go home with empty bags. When the last hymn of Sohila explains its urgent request, it reaches for exactly that language: profit, earning, buying, a short stay.
screen: `A MARKET TOWN, A SHORT STAY.` → `WHAT YOU EARN, YOU CARRY HOME.` → `THE HYMN SPEAKS LIKE A TRADER.`

segments.voice: Here's the request, in paraphrase. Listen, my friends: this is the time to serve the holy. Earn the profit of God here, and your dwelling hereafter will be easy. The word for profit is laahaa, an ordinary trader's word, gain at the end of the day. Then the urgency. In paraphrase again: day and night, life is running down; O mind, meet the Guru and set your affairs in order. That's a sentence anyone with a deadline understands. The hours are going whether you use them or not. The hymn goes on: this world is caught in corruption and doubt; the one who knows God crosses over. Buy what you came here to buy. Through the Guru, God comes to dwell in the mind, and you reach your own true home in ease, with no more coming and going. And then the very last request in the whole of Sohila. Guru Arjan asks for one thing. In paraphrase: Nanak, Your servant, begs for this happiness: make me the dust of the feet of the holy. So the night prayer ends on humility, the lowest place in the room, chosen on purpose. Here's why it belongs at bedtime. Night is when you count the day. What did I earn? Not money: kindness, attention, remembering. The hymn doesn't scold. It just says the market's still open. Tonight counts. Now is the time.
screen: `LAAHAA: THE DAY'S PROFIT.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, LIFE RUNS DOWN.` · `BUY WHAT YOU CAME TO BUY.` · `MAKE ME THE DUST OF THE HOLY'S FEET.` · then, large: `NOW IS THE TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one kind act before bed. Sit for a moment first and let one person come to mind: someone at home, someone you could text, someone you owe a thank-you. Decide one small thing you can do for them tonight. Fill a water glass. Leave a note. Send three warm words. Wash a dish that isn't yours. Picture yourself doing it. Then, when the bell ends, go and do it, before the day closes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once first. The bell holds the time.
Now is the time. Guru Arjan's request in Sohila's last hymn: listen, friends, life is running down day and night, so serve the holy and earn the profit of the Name today.
Your line: now is the time. Tonight, before you sleep, ask yourself the trader's question: what did I earn today that I can carry home? Day four hundred thirty-three.

434.word: A wedding song at a funeral
434.hook: Sohila is also sung at cremations, a song of the soul going home
434.howItsDone: At a Sikh cremation, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila and then the Ardas, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada directs; the same hymns are said by Sikhs every night before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was now is the time, and the trader's question: what did I earn today? This is a week's end too: the sky's aarti, the wind, the city of thieves, Guru Arjan's request. Today, where else Sohila is sung. Day four hundred thirty-four.
screen: `NOW IS THE TIME.` · `A WEEK: THE AARTI, THE CITY, THE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: A first-dance song at a graveside would stop a room cold. Yet at a Sikh cremation, once the fire is lit, the words recited sound, to anyone who knows them, like a wedding: the date written, oil poured at the threshold, friends asked for their blessings, a bride called to meet her Lord. It's Sohila, the same five hymns said at bedtime. Here the wedding words aren't a mistake. They're the point.
screen: `WEDDING MUSIC, FUNERAL MUSIC.` → `AT THE CREMATION: SOHILA.` → `THE SAME FIVE HYMNS AS LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets out the funeral. The body is washed and dressed, and the family gathers. At the cremation ground, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila, and then the Ardas is said. In the days that follow, a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or at a gurdwara. Sikh teaching also asks mourners not to give way to loud wailing. Grief is real, and tears are human, but the songs are of praise. So why Sohila, of all hymns? Go back to Sohila's first hymn. The date has been written. Friends, pour the oil, give your blessings, so I may meet my Lord. The summons goes to every house, every day. Read at the pyre, the funeral becomes the day that summons arrives for one soul, and the wedding in the hymn is the meeting with the Beloved. In the language of the hymn, the person who has died isn't lost to darkness. They're going home, the way a bride goes to her new home. Notice what that does to the night. If the same five hymns are sung at bedtime and at the end of a life, some readers hear every night as a small rehearsal: lying down, letting go of the day, trusting the morning to the One. And the last line of Sohila, sung at the pyre as well as at the pillow, is Guru Arjan asking to be the dust of the holy's feet. Even at the end, humility.
screen: `THE PYRE IS LIT; SOHILA IS SUNG.` · `PRAISE INSTEAD OF WAILING.` · `THE SUMMONS ARRIVES FOR ONE SOUL.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think kindly of someone who died. Let one person come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe someone you barely knew but remember. Picture their face as it was on a good day. Remember one thing they did well, one kindness, one habit, one laugh. If grief comes up, let it come; nothing needs fixing. Hold them in your mind like a friend at the door wishing a traveler well. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them, softly. The bell holds the time.
A wedding song at a funeral. Kirtan Sohila, sung at Sikh cremations as well as at bedtime: the soul as a bride, called to meet the Beloved and going home.
screen: `A WEDDING SONG AT A FUNERAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: going home. Tonight, as you lie down, let the day go the way the hymn lets a life go: with praise, and with trust. Day four hundred thirty-four.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sohila, a song of praise and joy; sung at bedtime and at the cremation ground.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's strange to sing about a wedding at a funeral.
what it means: in Sohila the soul is the bride and the wedding is the meeting with God, so the song fits the day a soul goes home.
what a scholar hears: the Sikh Rehat Maryada prescribes Kirtan Sohila and Ardas at the cremation, and discourages wailing; the first hymn itself calls what it sings a sohila, a song of praise.
